Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from Dr. Kaaki's lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no lung-cancer chapter. The Nov 2026 re-send of the slides is identical.

Objectives

  • Solitary pulmonary nodule · lung-cancer screening · approach to lung cancer: history, physical examination, investigations, staging, management.

1. Solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN)

  • Definition: a single, spherical, well-circumscribed radiologic opacity ≤ 3 cm, surrounded completely by normal lung. The patient is completely asymptomatic.
  • 0.2% incidentaloma finding on all CXR and CT chest.
  • ≤ 3 cm = nodule; > 3 cm = mass.
  • The cut-off to call a lung lesion a nodule → 3 cm or less. 439

Differential diagnosis — VITAMIN-O

Causes
V — vascularA-V malformation, pulmonary varix, haematoma, pulmonary infarct
I — infectionInfectious granuloma (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, TB, atypical mycobacteria, cryptococcosis, blastomycosis), bacterial abscess, Dirofilaria immitis, echinococcus (hydatid) cyst, ascariasis, Pneumocystis jirovecii, aspergillus
T — traumaContusion, penetration
A — autoimmuneWegener's (granulomatosis with polyangiitis), rheumatoid nodule, sarcoidosis
M — malformationCPAM, bronchogenic cyst, oesophageal cyst, duplication cyst, any chest cyst
I — inflammatoryWegener's, rheumatoid nodule, sarcoidosis
N — neoplasiaBenign: hamartoma, lipoma, fibroma, neurofibroma, leiomyoma, angioma · Malignant primary: adeno, SCC, large cell, small cell, carcinoid, extranodal lymphoma · Metastatic: breast, colon, melanoma (the 3 most common lung mets), head & neck, renal, sarcoma, germ cell; most common endobronchial mets: colon, breast, renal · Miscellaneous: plasmacytoma, schwannoma
O — othersAmyloidoma, rounded atelectasis, intrapulmonary lymph node, pseudotumour (loculated fluid), mucoid impaction
  • Independent predictors of malignancy: older age · current or previous smoker · history of extrathoracic cancer · diameter · spiculated margins · upper-lobe location.
  • Neoplastic branch: benign (hamartoma, granuloma) vs malignant primary vs secondary (e.g. colon → lung). A previous intrathoracic cancer suggests recurrence. Upper-lobe predominance is a probability, not a rule.
  • Malignant lung lesion → carcinoid tumour (a low-grade malignant neuroendocrine tumour; hamartoma, granular cell tumour and sclerosing haemangioma are benign). 429 ×3

2. Lung-cancer screening

  • WHO definition: screening is the presumptive identification of unrecognized disease in an apparently healthy, asymptomatic population by tests, examinations or procedures that can be applied rapidly and easily to the target population.
  • Benefit: early diagnosis.
A disease suitable for screening…The best screening test…
Has a significant negative impact on healthDetects a high proportion of disease in its preclinical state
Has an identifiable asymptomatic periodIs safe
Has improved outcomes with early interventionIs reasonable in cost
Has risk factorsLeads to demonstrated improved health outcomes
Is widely available — as are the interventions after a positive result
  • Why lung cancer? Curable at an early stage (survival: stage I 80% vs stage III 30%) · asymptomatic in early stages, symptoms nonspecific · a major health hazard · has risk factors · available modalities.
RisksBenefits
Futile detection of small aggressive tumours or indolent disease (overdiagnosis)Decreased lung-cancer mortality
Quality of life — anxiety of test findingsQuality of life — less disease- and treatment-related morbidity, healthier lifestyles, less anxiety
Physical complications from the diagnostic work-upDiscovery of other significant occult problems (thyroid nodule, silent coronary disease, early renal cancer, aortic aneurysm, breast cancer)
False positives and false negatives · unnecessary tests · radiation · cost · incidental lesions
  • Screening = asymptomatic target population, no known abnormality · surveillance = following a known abnormality · diagnosis = prompted by symptoms.
  • Evidence: CXR screening failed (small cancers aren't visible). NLST: low-dose CT → ~20% fewer lung-cancer deaths; a European trial (NELSON) ~30%.
  • Who gets screened (high risk): age ≥ 50 and ≥ 20 pack-years → annual low-dose CT. An abnormality moves the patient onto the nodule algorithm. Benefits outweigh risks only in the target population. Vaping, IQOS and shisha count as smoking.
  • Asymptomatic 52-year-old, 30 pack-years, quit 10 years ago → annual low-dose CT. 442
  • Screening candidate → 51-year-old with 30 pack-years (not < 20 pack-years, not < 50 years old). 441

3. Lung cancer

Types

  • Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC): adenocarcinoma · squamous cell carcinoma · adenosquamous carcinoma · large cell carcinoma · carcinoid tumours (typical and atypical).
  • Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC).
  • Neuroendocrine spectrum (best → worst prognosis): typical carcinoid → atypical carcinoid → large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma → small-cell carcinoma — same cell of origin, very different behaviour.
  • SCLC: most aggressive, presents at an advanced stage, usually non-resectable — but a very early, small localized SCLC (e.g. 2 cm) may be resected. Untreated advanced SCLC survival ≈ 6 months.
  • Lung cancer treated non-surgically → small cell carcinoma (chemo-radiotherapy). 438 ×2

Presentation

  • Symptomatic vs asymptomatic (screening) — asymptomatic 80%.
  • Cough, haemoptysis, recurrent respiratory infections, dyspnoea, chest pain.
  • The most common presentation of lung cancer → asymptomatic (incidental). 438

4. Work-up

  • History and physical examination · basic blood labs · CXR · CT chest (infused) · tissue biopsy · PET-CT · bronchoscopy, mediastinoscopy/EBUS · pulmonary function tests.
  • History: HPI (symptoms and risk factors), PMHx, PSHx, social history — smoking in detail, family history, allergies, medications.
  • Examination: inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation.
  • Smoking history: when started/stopped, packs per day, type. In a surgical candidate check anticoagulants and steroids. The exam is often normal in early disease. CT with IV contrast separates masses from vessels.

Investigations — to determine operability (patient) and resectability (cancer)

  • CXR · CT chest (infused) · tissue biopsy · PET-CT, MRI brain with contrast (stage II, IIIA; stage IB optional) · CT abdomen, bone scan (if PET-CT is not available or more information is needed) · bronchoscopy, mediastinoscopy/EBUS — for T2 (T1 has 5–7% mediastinal node mets), central tumours, enlarged LN, or PET-avid N1/N2 · PFTs.

Chest X-ray and contrast CT chest — lung mass

CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of a peripheral lesion

PET-CT — hypermetabolic primary tumour and nodes

Metastatic work-up — CT abdomen (liver mets), bone scan, brain MRI (enhancing metastasis)

  • Tissue diagnosis is non-negotiable — never give chemo/radiotherapy on imaging alone; diagnosis precedes staging. Peripheral lesion → CT-guided biopsy; central lesion → bronchoscopy.
  • Bronchoscopy is done routinely before resection — to find a synchronous endobronchial tumour and confirm bronchial anatomy.
  • PET-CT is for staging. Uptake ≠ cancer (infection/inflammation also light up). Brain, kidneys and bladder take up tracer physiologically → PET is unreliable for the brain: brain metastasis → MRI (contrast CT if MRI isn't possible).
  • Lung-cancer patient with headache, suspected metastasis → brain MRI. 439 ×2

Bronchoscopy, EBUS, EUS and mediastinoscopy

Bronchoscopy — endobronchial tumour

Transbronchial needle aspiration of a subcarinal node

EUS and trans-oesophageal FNA — linear echo-endoscope with a fine needle

Cervical mediastinoscopy — suprasternal incision, scope along the trachea

MethodHowReach / yield (notes)
EBUSBronchoscope with ultrasound; FNA under real-time ultrasound (a saline balloon couples the probe)Paratracheal, peribronchial nodes — less invasive
Bronchoscopic FNAFNA through a conventional bronchoscope, guided by anatomye.g. station 7 (subcarinal)
EUSUltrasound via the oesophagusPeri-oesophageal nodes
MediastinoscopySuprasternal incision, scope along the trachea, nodes biopsied directlyHighest tissue yield (whole nodes)
  • Complications of mediastinoscopy: major vascular injury (azygos vein → may need sternotomy) · oesophageal injury → mediastinitis · pneumothorax.
  • Most accurate statement on NSCLC staging → mediastinoscopy/mediastinotomy stages NSCLC with > 90% accuracy (fixed — the recall keyed "VATS is used routinely", which is not true; CT chest is always needed, MRI is not superior). 436

5. Staging

TNM 8th edition — primary tumour, nodes and metastasis, and the stage grouping table

N stageAnatomyImplication (notes)
N1Ipsilateral hilar / intrapulmonaryResect first; adjuvant chemotherapy after
N2Ipsilateral mediastinalChanges initial management — neoadjuvant therapy → reassess → resection in selected patients
N3Contralateral mediastinal/hilar (or supraclavicular)Usually inoperable

6. Treatment — based on the stage

  • Stage I: surgery only (small tumour, no LN or distant mets).
  • Stage II and IIIA: surgery with adjuvant or neoadjuvant treatment (chemotherapy and radiation therapy).
  • Stage IIIB and above: chemotherapy and radiation therapy, palliation.
  • Stage II–III treatment is multimodal (surgery, chemo, radiation, targeted therapy, immunotherapy). Stage IV (distant mets) → systemic and palliative treatment.
  • Resectability = tumour/stage; operability = patient/function (PFTs). Curative surgery needs both.

Surgical treatment

  • Pre-operative assessment: general health status · lung function (PFTs, VO₂ max, ABG, V/Q scan).
  • Anatomical resection (take the vein, artery and bronchus with the lymph nodes): segmentectomy · lobectomy · pneumonectomy.
  • Not wedge resection (non-anatomical).
  • Lobectomy is the workhorse for lung cancer; pneumonectomy is not done just because cancer is present. Wedge resection = non-anatomical — for diagnosis, benign lesions and pulmonary metastases (e.g. colon cancer mets). Use the least lung resection that is oncologically adequate.
  • Early NSCLC of the right lower lobe (T1N0M0) → right lower lobectomy. 437 ×7
  • Wedge resection is best indicated for → lung metastasis (not primary lung cancer). 436

Approaches

  • Thoracotomy · VATS · RATS (robotic).

Thoracotomy — open incision; post-thoracotomy scar with chest drains

VATS — port sites and the operating team

  • Priorities: 1) complete cancer resection, 2) patient safety — converting to thoracotomy is right whenever it serves these. Thoracotomy is very painful (intercostal injury, more than sternotomy) → poor breathing → pneumonia.
  • VATS: multi-port (3–4 ports) or uniportal (fewer intercostal spaces, potentially less pain) — no proven superiority of either. Robotic: articulated instruments, 3D view, seated ergonomics — minimally invasive for the patient. One chest tube is usually left after resection.

7. Palliative care

  • Pain · pleural effusion · haemoptysis.
  • Palliative ≠ do nothing: pain → pain specialist/analgesia · effusion → drainage · haemoptysis → bronchoscopic/endobronchial intervention.
Title-slide picture fragments (10)

Mastery checklist (notes)

  • ≤ 3 cm = nodule; > 3 cm = mass; an SPN is an incidental finding in an asymptomatic patient.
  • Screening = asymptomatic target population; surveillance = known abnormality; diagnosis = symptoms.
  • Age ≥ 50 + ≥ 20 pack-years → annual LDCT; NLST ~20% mortality reduction; CXR screening failed.
  • SPN malignancy predictors: age, smoking, prior cancer, diameter, spiculation, upper lobe.
  • Typical carcinoid = best prognosis; SCLC = worst; SCLC usually non-resectable.
  • Tissue before treatment; diagnosis before staging. Peripheral → CT-guided biopsy; central → bronchoscopy.
  • PET uptake ≠ cancer; brain mets → MRI.
  • N1 → resect + adjuvant chemo; N2 → changes initial management; N3 → usually inoperable.
  • EBUS less invasive; mediastinoscopy higher yield (risks: azygos injury, oesophageal injury).
  • Resectability = tumour; operability = patient.
  • Cancer → anatomical resection (lobectomy); wedge = diagnosis, benign disease, metastases.
  • Palliation: analgesia, drainage of effusion, bronchoscopic control of haemoptysis.
